verses.text: All the kings across the Jordan heard what had happened. They were the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, from the hill country, the lowlands, and all along the coast of the great sea toward Lebanon.
They united to fight against Joshua and Israel.
But when the people of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai,
they came up with a trick. They posed as ambassadors and loaded their donkeys with worn-out sacks and old wineskins that had split and been tied back together.
They put on old clothes and worn-out, patched sandals. All the bread they'd packed for the journey was dry and moldy.
They went to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal and told him and the Israelites, “We've come from far away. Make a treaty with us.”
The Israelites asked the Hivites, “What if you live right here among us? How could we make a treaty with you?”
They said to Joshua, “We're your servants.” Joshua asked, “Who are you, and where are you from?”
They answered, “Your servants have come from a very distant country because of the name of the LORD your God. We've heard about him and everything he did in Egypt.
We also heard what he did to both Amorite kings beyond the Jordan: King Sihon of Heshbon and King Og of Bashan, who ruled at Ashtaroth.
Our elders and everyone in our country told us, ‘Pack food for the trip and go meet them. Tell them, “We're your servants. Please make a treaty with us.”’
This bread was still hot when we packed it at home the day we left to come to you. Look at it now. It's dry and moldy.
These wineskins were new when we filled them, and look how torn they are now. Our clothes and sandals wore out because the trip was so long.”
The Israelites sampled their supplies without asking the LORD for guidance.
Joshua made peace with them and signed a treaty promising to let them live. The leaders of the community swore to keep it.
Three days after they made the treaty, the Israelites found out these people were their neighbors and lived right among them.
The Israelites set out and reached their towns on the third day. The towns were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim.
The Israelites didn't attack them, because the leaders of the community had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. The whole community complained against the leaders.
But the leaders told the whole community, “We've sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. We can't touch them now.
Here's what we'll do: we'll let them live, so God's anger won't come on us for breaking the oath we swore to them.”
The leaders said, “Let them live.” So the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole community, just as the leaders said.
Joshua called them in and asked, “Why did you deceive us by saying, ‘We live far away,’ when you live right among us?
Now you're under a curse. Some of you will always serve as slaves, cutting wood and carrying water for the house of my God.”

They answered Joshua, “Your servants were told for certain that the LORD your God commanded his servant Moses to give you this whole land and destroy everyone living in it ahead of you. We were scared for our lives because of you. That's why we did it.
Now we're in your hands. Do whatever you think is good and right.”
Joshua did as he said. He rescued them from the Israelites, who otherwise would have killed them.
That day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the community and for the LORD's altar at the place the LORD would choose. They still do that work today.
